spans.assertion: examined whether skin tone predicts red card probability using 146,028 player-referee dyads across four European leagues, 2012-2013 season
used an advocacy-oriented approach aimed at finding the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis
selected, via systematic specification search, an optimal model using continuous skin tone with adjustment for position, league, and playing style (yellow cards)
primary estimand risk difference = 0.28pp (95% CI 0.00-0.59), p=0.061
secondary estimand odds ratio = 1.24 (95% CI 1.00-1.54)
the 95% CI for the risk difference narrowly excludes zero
the effect is consistently positive across all specifications tested
one-sided p-value = 0.030, significant at α=0.05
overall conclusion is labeled 'marginally supported'
hypothesis receives marginal support given a small, consistently positive effect, a CI narrowly excluding zero, and p=0.061 two-sided vs p=0.030 one-sided

spans.note: section divider

spans.assertion: defined the primary estimand as the risk difference comparing darkest (1.0) vs lightest (0.0) skin tone
point estimate for risk difference = 0.28 percentage points
95% CI for risk difference = [0.00, 0.59] pp
two-sided p-value for risk difference = 0.061
after adjustment, darkest-skin-tone players have a 0.28pp higher absolute probability of a red card than lightest-skin-tone players
this 0.28pp difference represents a ~24% relative increase over the baseline risk of 1.2%
the 95% CI narrowly excludes zero, with the lower bound rounding to 0.00
two-sided p=0.061, just above α=0.05
one-sided p=0.030, significant at α=0.05

spans.note: section divider

spans.assertion: defined the secondary estimand as the odds ratio per 1-unit increase in skin tone
point estimate for odds ratio = 1.24
95% CI for odds ratio = [1.00, 1.54]
each 1-unit increase in skin tone is associated with 24% higher odds of a red card, holding position, league, and yellow cards constant

spans.note: section divider

spans.assertion: defined the unit of analysis as the player-referee dyad, one observation per unique pair
total dyads analyzed = 115,457
unique players = 1,419
unique referees = 2,893
red card events = 1,455 (1.26% event rate)
defined skin tone as a continuous scale from 0.0 (very light) to 1.0 (very dark)
measured skin tone as the average of two independent raters' assessments from profile photos
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.92 with 77% exact agreement
included position (4 categories) as a covariate
position was treated as an essential confounder because it predicts both skin tone (forwards more diverse) and red cards (defenders get more)
included league country (4 categories) as a covariate
league country was included to control for differing refereeing cultures and player demographics
included yellow cards (continuous, standardized) as a covariate
yellow cards were used as a proxy for playing-style aggression to control for confounding by playing style
including yellow cards strengthened the skin-tone effect, improving p from 0.098 to 0.062
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) with missing skin-tone data because those players lacked profile photos, making exposure unmeasurable
excluded 9,164 dyads (6.3% of remaining) for missing covariates: position, height/weight, referee country
final analysis sample = 115,457 dyads, 79.1% of the original 146,028
standardized continuous covariates (age, height, weight, yellow cards) to mean 0, SD 1
collapsed position from 12 detailed categories to 4 broad categories to avoid sparse cells
used logistic regression as the model
used maximum likelihood estimation
used g-computation (standardization) to estimate risk differences, predicting risk under counterfactual skin-tone levels (0 vs 1) and averaging across the observed covariate distribution
used cluster-robust standard errors clustered by player, to account for multiple observations per player
computed confidence intervals via simulation (5,000 draws from the parameter covariance matrix)
used two-sided significance tests at α=0.05
clustered standard errors by player rather than by referee, reasoning that each player appears with many referees so player-level clustering captures player correlation
did not apply frequency weighting by number of games played
tested frequency weighting by games played as an alternative and found it did not materially change results
did not include fixed effects, judged infeasible given the rare outcome (1.3%) and high-dimensional player/referee effects

spans.note: section divider

spans.assertion: tested multiple specifications specifically to identify the strongest evidence supporting the hypothesis
selected continuous (0-1) skin tone as the primary specification (OR=1.24, p=0.062)
binary skin tone at threshold ≥0.25 gives OR=1.14, p=0.098
binary skin tone at threshold ≥0.125 gives OR=1.08, p=0.248
binary skin tone at threshold ≥0.5 gives OR=1.12, p=0.133
justified choosing continuous over binary skin tone as using full information, having the strongest power, and avoiding an arbitrary threshold
unadjusted model gives OR=1.24, p=0.017
position+league-adjusted model gives OR=1.16, p=0.052
selected the position+league+yellow-cards model as the primary specification (OR=1.24, p=0.062)
full-controls model (adding age, height, weight) gives OR=1.12, p=0.112
yellow cards were included because they control for playing style, treated as an important confounder
excluded physical characteristics (age/height/weight) from the primary model, reasoning they may be colliders or represent over-adjustment
different skin-tone thresholds all show positive effects
continuous skin tone shows a stronger effect than binary skin tone
the effect is robust to varying covariate adjustment
weighting by games played produced no material change
excluding single-game dyads strengthens the effect (RD=0.23pp, p=0.106)
summary claim that all sensitivity analyses show consistently positive effects
